reference.source: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine / AASLD & ACG
clinicalPearls: A malabsorptive state resulting from loss of functional small-intestinal length, usually after extensive surgical resection for conditions such as mesenteric ischaemia, Crohn disease, trauma, or radiation injury
Clinical severity depends on the length and site of remaining bowel, whether the ileocaecal valve and colon are preserved, and the health of the residual intestine
The main manifestations are diarrhoea, steatorrhoea, dehydration, electrolyte disturbance, weight loss, and specific nutrient deficiencies
Loss of the terminal ileum impairs absorption of vitamin B12 and bile salts, and bile-salt spillage into the colon can worsen diarrhoea and predispose to gallstones
An intact colon is nutritionally valuable because it salvages energy by fermenting malabsorbed carbohydrate into short-chain fatty acids
Over months to years the residual bowel undergoes adaptation, increasing absorptive capacity, so nutritional needs may lessen with time
Management is staged: fluid and electrolyte correction, parenteral nutrition when needed, gradual introduction of enteral feeding to drive adaptation, and dietary modification
Long-term parenteral nutrition carries important complications including catheter-related bloodstream infection, venous thrombosis, and intestinal-failure-associated liver disease
Enterohormonal therapy (such as GLP-2 analogues) and, in selected refractory cases, intestinal transplantation are options for those dependent on parenteral support
reference.pathophysiology: Short bowel syndrome arises when the absorptive surface of the small intestine is reduced below the level needed to maintain nutrition and hydration, most often after massive resection. The functional consequences depend on which segment is lost: jejunal loss reduces overall absorptive surface, while ileal loss additionally impairs vitamin B12 and bile-salt reabsorption, disrupting the enterohepatic circulation and causing bile-salt diarrhoea and fat malabsorption. Loss of the ileocaecal valve accelerates transit and predisposes to small-intestinal bacterial overgrowth. Rapid transit and reduced surface lead to fluid, electrolyte, and nutrient losses. Over time the remnant intestine adapts through mucosal hyperplasia and slowed transit, partially restoring absorptive capacity.
additionalDifferentials: Coeliac disease and other mucosal malabsorptive disorders
Inflammatory bowel disease with active malabsorption
Enteric fistula causing functional bowel loss
additionalInvestigations: Assessment of remaining bowel anatomy and length from operative records and imaging
Nutritional and electrolyte panel including magnesium, calcium, and trace elements
Fat-soluble vitamin, vitamin B12, and iron status
Monitoring of fluid balance and stool or stoma output
Liver function monitoring in patients on parenteral nutrition and evaluation for bacterial overgrowth
redFlags: Severe dehydration with acute kidney injury or dangerous electrolyte disturbances
Catheter-related bloodstream infection or sepsis in patients on parenteral nutrition
Progressive intestinal-failure-associated liver disease or cholestasis
Central venous thrombosis threatening long-term access for parenteral nutrition
reference.prognosis: Outlook depends on residual bowel length and anatomy and on adaptation. Many patients eventually achieve enteral autonomy, while those with very short remnants or absent colon may need lifelong parenteral nutrition, whose complications (liver disease, line sepsis, thrombosis) drive much of the long-term morbidity and mortality.
pitfalls: Underestimating fluid and electrolyte losses, particularly magnesium, in high-output patients
Withholding enteral nutrition entirely and thereby delaying adaptation
Overlooking vitamin B12 and fat-soluble vitamin deficiency after ileal resection
Missing small-intestinal bacterial overgrowth or catheter sepsis as causes of deterioration
management: Parenteral nutrition and intravenous fluid and electrolyte support initially to prevent dehydration and malnutrition, weaning as intestinal adaptation allows
Structured enteral and oral nutrition to stimulate adaptation, with the diet tailored to remnant anatomy and whether the colon is in continuity
Antidiarrhoeal and antisecretory agents (loperamide, and proton pump inhibitors for gastric hypersecretion) to slow transit and reduce output
Bile-acid sequestrants for bile-salt diarrhoea and parenteral vitamin B12 replacement after terminal ileal loss
The GLP-2 analogue teduglutide to enhance intestinal absorption and reduce parenteral nutrition dependence in selected patients
Correct and monitor micronutrient, fat-soluble vitamin, and trace-element deficiencies
Surveillance for parenteral-nutrition complications (intestinal failure-associated liver disease, catheter sepsis, thrombosis) and small-intestinal bacterial overgrowth
Manage in a specialist intestinal failure multidisciplinary team, considering surgical lengthening or intestinal transplantation for refractory cases
